newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nintendo suffers sharp dive in half-year profits.
newsitem.headline: Nintendo suffers sharp dive in half-year profits.

text.p: A shift to new-generation videogame machines slashed industry giant Nintendo Co. Ltd's six-month profits in half, but the Christmas shopping rush will make its full-year earnings less gloomy.
The launch of the smarter and faster 64-bit game machine, N64, in June apparently came too late to stop a hefty decline in parent profits in the April-September period, the company said Tuesday.
Nintendo said its half-year current profit plunged 53 percent from a year ago to 30 billion yen ($263 million), while its sales slipped 3.7 percent to 130.16 billion yen ($1.14 billion).

For the full year to March, the company saw a 27 percent year-on-year drop in its current profit to 85 billion yen ($745 million), but a rise of 13 percent in sales to 340 billion yen ($2.98 billion).
Current profit is pretax and includes gains or losses on non-operating activities such as investment in stocks.

Nintendo is in what some analysts termed an "off-crop season." Its profits are being hurt in the short-term because the launch of the new, higher-performance player has resulted in falling prices for software for Nintendo's old SuperFamicon player, which is still the company's mainstay product.
Nintendo's second-half performance will win close attention, as the year-end gift-giving season typically accounts for 60 percent of videogame makers' sales.
Analysts said Nintendo's N64 would battle head-to-head with Sony Corp.'s PlayStation this Christmas, and outperform Sega Enterprise Ltd's Saturn player.

Nintendo spokesman Hiroshi Imanishi said the company hopes to sell four million of its 64-bit machines at home and abroad by the end of the year. It also hopes to sell a total of six million units by end-March.
"In the face of high popularity in the United States and a likely rise in demand there during the Christmas season, we modified our N64 shipments plan," he told reporters.

Nintendo's shipments of the new game player for the April-June period totalled 1.16 million in Japan and 800,000 in the United States. It had originally counted on shipments of 1.80 million units in Japan and 200,000 in the United States.

On a group basis, Nintendo said it had net profit of 48 billion yen ($421 million) for 1996/97, unchanged from its May forecast, while it raised its sales forecast to 395 billion yen ($3.46 billion), up 10 billion yen ($87.7 million) from its May forecast.
In the year to March 1996, it posted net group profit of 59.9 billion yen ($525 million).
In contrast to unexpectedly slow sales of the N64 at home, which analysts blame on a lack of attractive software, Nintendo enjoyed soaring demand for its new product among Americans.
Early last month, Nintendo said its entire 350,000-unit shipment of N64s had sold out in U.S. stores just three days after their launch in late September.

The cutting-edge 64-bit player, which improves on the graphics and speed of its 16-bit system, is crucial for Nintendo's bid to recapture the top spot in the hotly competitive $11 billion-a-year U.S. video game market.
